texts.title: The rise of remote work
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: The shift towards remote work, accelerated by the global pandemic, has fundamentally changed how companies operate. While many employers initially feared a drop in productivity, studies have consistently shown the opposite. Employees working from home often report higher job satisfaction and better work-life balance. Nevertheless, remote work is not without its challenges. Isolation and the blurring of boundaries between professional and personal life are common complaints. Some companies have responded by adopting hybrid models, allowing employees to split their time between the office and home. This approach appears to offer the best of both worlds, though it requires careful management to ensure team cohesion is maintained. The future of work, it seems, will be defined by flexibility rather than rigid structures.

texts.title: The psychology of habits
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Habits are powerful forces in our lives. Research suggests that around 40 percent of our daily actions are not conscious decisions but habits. This means that much of our behaviour is automatic, triggered by cues in our environment. Understanding how habits work can help us change them. Every habit has three components: a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue triggers the behaviour, the routine is the behaviour itself, and the reward is the positive feeling we get. To change a habit, we need to keep the cue and the reward but replace the routine. For example, if you want to stop eating sweets when you are stressed, you could replace that behaviour with a short walk, which also reduces stress. Changing habits is not easy, but it is possible with patience and consistency.

texts.title: The future of artificial intelligence
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Artificial intelligence is transforming almost every industry, from healthcare to transport. AI systems can now diagnose diseases, drive cars and even write articles. Supporters argue that AI will make our lives easier and more efficient, freeing us from repetitive tasks. However, critics warn that AI could destroy millions of jobs, especially in sectors like manufacturing and customer service. There is also concern about privacy, as AI systems collect enormous amounts of personal data. Some experts believe that governments need to create clear rules to ensure AI is used responsibly. Others argue that slowing down AI development would be a mistake, as it could give an advantage to countries with fewer ethical restrictions. The debate is likely to continue for many years.

texts.title: The benefits of failure
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: In modern society, failure is often seen as something to be avoided at all costs. However, many psychologists argue that failure is actually a necessary part of learning and growth. When we fail, we are forced to reflect on what went wrong and adjust our approach. Some of the most successful people in history failed many times before achieving their goals. J.K. Rowling was rejected by twelve publishers before Harry Potter was accepted. Steve Jobs was fired from Apple, the company he founded. What these examples show is that failure is not the opposite of success - it is part of it. The key is to see failure as feedback rather than as a final verdict on your abilities. People who develop this mindset are more likely to take risks, learn from mistakes and ultimately succeed.

texts.title: The rise of electric cars
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Electric cars are becoming increasingly popular around the world. Governments in many countries are offering financial incentives to encourage people to switch from petrol and diesel vehicles. The main advantage of electric cars is that they produce no direct emissions, which helps to improve air quality in cities. They are also cheaper to run, since electricity costs less than petrol. However, there are still significant obstacles. The biggest one is the limited range of most electric vehicles, which makes long journeys difficult. Charging infrastructure is also inadequate in many areas, and charging times are much longer than refuelling a traditional car. Battery production raises environmental concerns too, since mining lithium and cobalt has a considerable impact. Despite these challenges, most experts agree that electric cars are the future of transport.

texts.title: The importance of sleep
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Sleep is essential for our physical and mental health, yet many people treat it as optional. Research shows that adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep per night, but a significant proportion of the population regularly gets less than this. The consequences of sleep deprivation are serious. In the short term, it affects concentration, mood and decision-making. In the long term, it increases the risk of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. Unfortunately, modern life is not designed for good sleep. Screens, artificial light and irregular schedules all interfere with our natural sleep cycle. Experts recommend establishing a consistent bedtime routine, avoiding caffeine in the afternoon and keeping the bedroom dark and cool. Some people also benefit from avoiding screens for an hour before bed. The message is clear: sleep is not a luxury, it is a necessity.

texts.title: Is social media making us lonely?
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Social media was supposed to bring people closer together. In theory, we can now communicate with friends and family anywhere in the world, share experiences and build communities. Yet many researchers are noticing a paradox: despite being more connected than ever, many people report feeling lonelier. One explanation is that online interactions are not a substitute for face-to-face contact. A brief exchange of messages does not provide the same emotional benefits as a real conversation. Another issue is comparison. Social media shows us a constant stream of other people's highlight reels, which can make our own lives feel inadequate. However, the relationship is complex. For some people, especially those who are isolated or have limited mobility, social media provides a lifeline. The impact depends largely on how we use these platforms - passively scrolling tends to have negative effects, while active engagement with real friends is generally positive.

texts.title: The value of boredom
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: In our modern world, boredom has become something to avoid at all costs. The moment we feel a hint of it, we reach for our phones. Yet a growing body of research suggests that boredom may actually be valuable. When we are bored, our minds wander, and this mental wandering is essential for creativity. Some of our best ideas come not when we are actively trying to solve a problem, but when we are doing something mundane, like taking a shower or walking the dog. Neuroscientists have found that during these idle moments, the brain is far from inactive. It is busy connecting ideas, consolidating memories and processing emotions. By constantly filling every moment with stimulation, we may be depriving ourselves of this important mental processing time. Perhaps the solution is not to eliminate boredom, but to embrace it.

texts.title: The ethics of fast fashion
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: Fast fashion has transformed the clothing industry. Brands can now design, produce and sell new collections in a matter of weeks, offering consumers cheap and trendy clothes. But this convenience comes at a price. The environmental impact is severe: the fashion industry is one of the largest polluters in the world, responsible for around 10 percent of global carbon emissions. It also consumes enormous amounts of water and produces vast quantities of textile waste. The human cost is equally troubling. Many garments are produced in factories where workers earn low wages and face unsafe conditions. Some consumers are starting to reject fast fashion in favour of sustainable alternatives, such as buying second-hand clothes or choosing brands that pay fair wages. However, sustainable fashion is often more expensive, which makes it inaccessible for people on low incomes. Solving this problem will require systemic change, not just individual choices.

texts.title: The science of happiness
texts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer A, B, C or D.
texts.text: What makes people happy? This question has fascinated philosophers for centuries, but in recent decades, psychologists have started to study it scientifically. Their findings are surprising. Contrary to popular belief, money has a limited effect on happiness once basic needs are met. Studies show that above a certain income level, additional money does not significantly increase life satisfaction. What matters more are relationships. People with strong social connections report being consistently happier than those who are isolated. Acts of kindness also have a measurable effect: helping others increases our own sense of well-being. Interestingly, the pursuit of happiness itself can be counterproductive. People who constantly ask themselves whether they are happy tend to feel less satisfied than those who simply engage in meaningful activities. In other words, happiness is often a by-product of a life well-lived, not a goal to be pursued directly.
